323.title: The second generation
323.hook: children grow up with Punjabi at home, other languages outside, and Gurmukhi classes at weekends
323.howItsDone: Many gurdwaras outside India run weekend Punjabi and Gurmukhi classes, kirtan lessons and youth camps so children can read the Guru Granth Sahib and feel at home in both worlds.

segments.voice: Yesterday, langar where disaster strikes: rice, dal and tea at borders and floods, and your line, the kitchen travels. Did you give a meal or a gift? Today, the kids who grew up eating that langar, far from Punjab. Day three hundred twenty-three.

Saturday morning, a gurdwara in Toronto, or Leicester, or Melbourne, or California. In a side room, a dozen kids sit at folding tables with notebooks, tracing curly letters while a patient teacher says each sound out loud. They'd rather be asleep, or at soccer. At home they speak Punjabi with their grandparents, English with their siblings, and something in between with their parents. At school, someone asks about the patka on a boy's head for the hundredth time. Today: the second generation.
screen: `SATURDAY MORNING, A SIDE ROOM.` → `TRACING CURLY LETTERS.` → `PUNJABI AT HOME, ENGLISH OUTSIDE.`

segments.voice: The children of Sikh immigrants grow up living in two worlds at once. At home: Punjabi, parathas, the Guru Granth Sahib in the front room or a picture of the Gurus on the wall, early morning prayers played from a phone. Outside: school, friends, sports, a whole other language and way of doing things. Many learn to switch between them without even noticing. Some feel pulled in two directions. Some cut their hair as teenagers, and some of those grow it back later. Some take amrit young. Most are somewhere in between, working it out. That's why the weekend Gurmukhi class matters so much. Gurmukhi is the script of the Guru Granth Sahib. Its name means from the mouth of the Guru. Tradition says the second Guru, Guru Angad, shaped and spread it, and taught children to read, so ordinary people could read the Guru's words for themselves. So when a kid in Toronto traces those letters on a Saturday, they're doing something Guru Angad did with children five hundred years ago. It's not just a language lesson. It's a key to the Guru. And the second generation has given something back. They've made Sikh camps, youth groups, podcasts and videos, and learned to explain the turban, the langar and the Gurus to their friends, often better than their parents could. They carry two worlds. But many of them will tell you there's one heart underneath it: the same Guru, the same sangat, just speaking more than one language. Two worlds, one heart.
screen: `TWO WORLDS AT ONCE.` · `WORKING IT OUT, AT EVERY STAGE.` · `GURMUKHI: FROM THE GURU'S MOUTH.` · `GIVING SOMETHING BACK.` · then, large: `TWO WORLDS, ONE HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say one word in another language. Settle, and breathe. Choose a word from a language that isn't your main one: a word you learned on this path, like sangat, or seva, or a word a friend taught you, or one from your grandparents. Say it quietly. Notice how it feels in your mouth, a little strange, a little warm. Think of someone who lives between two languages every day. Hold them kindly. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The second generation. Children of Sikh immigrants who grow up with Punjabi at home, other languages outside, and Gurmukhi on the weekends.
Your line: two worlds, one heart. Today, ask someone who grew up between two cultures what they love about each. Day three hundred twenty-three.

324.title: Kirtan in new places
324.hook: hymns now sound in gurdwaras on every continent, in old ragas and new voices
324.howItsDone: Kirtan is sung in every gurdwara, usually with harmonium and tabla, and more and more with stringed instruments; the kirtan from the Harmandir Sahib is broadcast daily for Sikhs around the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the second generation: Saturday Gurmukhi classes, Punjabi at home, and your line, two worlds, one heart. Today, the thing that sounds the same in both worlds: the Guru's song. Day three hundred twenty-four.

Somewhere in the world, right now, someone is singing the Guru's hymns. Early morning in Amritsar, the kirtan at the Harmandir Sahib has already begun. In Nairobi, a family is gathering. In Vancouver it's night, and a teenager is practicing on a harmonium, wearing headphones so she won't wake her little brother. In a gurdwara in Kuala Lumpur, a group of old men is singing along with a tabla. Follow the sun around the planet, and the song never stops. Today: kirtan in new places.
screen: `SOMEONE IS SINGING RIGHT NOW.` → `AMRITSAR, NAIROBI, VANCOUVER.` → `THE SONG NEVER STOPS.`

segments.voice: Kirtan means singing the praise of God, and for Sikhs it means singing the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib. It began with Guru Nanak and his companion Bhai Mardana, a Muslim musician who played the rabab, a stringed instrument, while the Guru sang. From the start, the Guru's word was meant to be sung. That's why the Guru Granth Sahib is arranged not by author or subject, but by raag: musical modes, each with its own mood and time of day. There are thirty-one main raags in it. Some are for dawn, some for evening, some for longing, some for joy. Over the centuries, the instruments changed. The harmonium, brought to India by Europeans in the 1800s, became the most common sound in gurdwaras. Recently, many young musicians have gone back to the old stringed instruments the Gurus' musicians played: the rabab, the dilruba, the taus. So kirtan today is both: old raags, and new voices. The diaspora has carried it everywhere. Kirtan now sounds in gurdwaras on every continent, in classrooms and camps, on phones and livestreams. The kirtan from the Harmandir Sahib is broadcast every day, so a grandmother in England can listen along with Amritsar at breakfast. Children learn the tabla in the same gurdwaras where their parents learned to read Gurmukhi. And people who aren't Sikh often find they love it too, even before they understand a word. The Gurus taught that the Name is sung, not only studied. And now that song is everywhere.
screen: `NANAK SINGS, MARDANA PLAYS.` · `ARRANGED BY RAAG, NOT BY AUTHOR.` · `HARMONIUM, AND OLD STRINGS REVIVED.` · `EVERY CONTINENT, EVERY SCREEN.` · then, large: `THE SONG EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to kirtan from far away. If you can, find a recording of kirtan, or the live broadcast from the Harmandir Sahib, and play it softly. If you can't right now, remember any kirtan you've heard on this path. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to follow the words. Just let the sound come to you from far away, the way it reaches millions of people every day. Let it hold your attention. When your mind wanders, come back to the sound. The bell holds the time.
Kirtan in new places. The Guru's hymns, sung in old raags and new voices, now sound in gurdwaras and homes on every continent.
Your line: the song everywhere. Today, when you hear music, remember that somewhere on earth, right now, someone is singing the Guru's hymns. Day three hundred twenty-four.

325.title: No stranger anywhere
325.hook: no one is my enemy and no one a stranger; I get along with all (Kanara, ang 1299)
325.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Arjan's hymn in Raag Kanara (Ang 1299) in kirtan, and many quote its line 'na ko bairi nahi bigana' as a summary of how the Gurus asked them to see others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan in new places: old raags, new voices, and your line, the song everywhere. Today, one line from that song that the whole diaspora could have written on its suitcases. Day three hundred twenty-five.

Think about the first day in a new place. A new school, a new job, a new country. Everyone else knows where the bathrooms are and who sits with whom. You're the stranger. And think of the other side: the day a stranger walks into your place, and you have to decide whether to smile. For two weeks we've followed Sikhs who were strangers almost everywhere they went: Hong Kong, Vancouver, Stockton, Southall. Today, a line from Guru Arjan that turns the whole idea of stranger inside out. Today: no stranger anywhere.
screen: `THE FIRST DAY IN A NEW PLACE.` → `WHETHER TO SMILE.` → `A LINE FROM GURU ARJAN.`

segments.voice: The hymn is by Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, in Raag Kanara, on page one thousand two hundred ninety-nine of the Guru Granth Sahib. It begins with a confession. I've forgotten all my envy of others, the Guru says, since I found the company of the holy. Then comes the line: Na ko bairi nahi bigana, sagal sang ham kau ban aai. No one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. I get along with everyone. Listen to the words. Bairi is an enemy. Bigana is a stranger, an outsider, someone who isn't one of us. And the Guru says there aren't any. Not because everyone is nice, but because of what comes next in the hymn: the one God is present in everyone, and seeing that, again and again, Nanak blossoms. If the same light is in every face, then nobody is a stranger. Just someone you haven't met. Notice where this comes from: the sangat. The Guru says this way of seeing arrived with holy company. You don't get there alone, by thinking. You get there by sitting with people. That's exactly what the diaspora did. They came as strangers to Malaya and Canada and California and Britain. They were turned away from harbors, refused citizenship, told to take off their turbans, attacked. And again and again they opened a room, installed the Guru, cooked langar, and fed whoever walked in, including the people who had treated them as strangers. That closes our look at the diaspora: from leaving Punjab to kitchens at every border. No one is a stranger.
screen: `GURU ARJAN, RAAG KANARA, ANG 1299.` · `NO ENEMY, NO STRANGER.` · `THE ONE LIGHT IN EVERY FACE.` · `LEARNED IN THE SANGAT.` · then, large: `NO ONE IS A STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: greet a stranger warmly, first in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Picture someone you'll probably see today but don't know: a cashier, a bus driver, a new face at work, someone on your street. See their face as clearly as you can. Now picture yourself greeting them the way you'd greet a cousin you haven't seen in a while. A real smile. Their name, if you know it. Notice what shifts in you. The bell holds the time.
No stranger anywhere. Guru Arjan's line: no one is my enemy and no one a stranger; I get along with all.
Your line: no one is a stranger. Today, greet one stranger warmly, as if they were already family. Day three hundred twenty-five.

326.title: Looking back: the stories
326.hook: ten Gurus, the sakhis, the Khalsa's birth: which story stayed with you
326.howItsDone: Sikh families tell sakhis, stories of the Gurus, to children at home and in gurdwara classes, and katha (explanation) in the gurdwara often retells a sakhi alongside the day's hymn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, no stranger anywhere: Guru Arjan's line, no enemy and no stranger, and your line, no one is a stranger. Did you greet someone warmly? Today we start climbing to the lookout at the end of the year, and look back. Day three hundred twenty-six.

Imagine someone at dinner asks you: so what have you actually learned on this path? You could list facts. Or you could tell them a story. A man who walked into a river and didn't come out for three days. A carpenter's plain bread, and a rich man's feast. A nine-year-old who told his father no one was more worthy than him. A sword drawn before a crowd, and five people who stood up. The stories are how most people carry a faith. This week, we look back at the whole year, and we start with them. Today: looking back.
screen: `WHAT HAVE YOU LEARNED?` → `A RIVER, A LOAF, A SWORD.` → `THE STORIES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Camp two was the stories, and they came in a line of ten Gurus. Guru Nanak, three days in the river Bein, coming out to say there is no Hindu and no Muslim. Eating Bhai Lalo's honest bread and refusing Malik Bhago's feast. Walking the world with Mardana and his rabab, then farming at Kartarpur. Guru Angad, shaping the Gurmukhi letters, while Mata Khivi ran the kitchen. Guru Amar Das, the old man who carried water before dawn, and who asked everyone, even an emperor, to eat in the langar first. Guru Ram Das, digging the pool at Amritsar. Guru Arjan, building a temple with four doors and gathering the hymns into one book, then becoming the first Sikh martyr. Guru Hargobind, wearing two swords. Guru Har Rai and his herb garden. Guru Har Krishan, a child nursing the sick in Delhi. Guru Tegh Bahadur, giving his life for the freedom of people of another faith. And Guru Gobind Singh: Vaisakhi, 1699, the sword, the five beloved, sugar stirred into water in an iron bowl, and the Guru asking the five to initiate him. And at the end, in 1708, the Guru passing the Guruship to the Granth. The word for these stories is sakhi. A sakhi is a story of the Gurus, and the word is linked to an old word for a witness. That's what a good sakhi does. It doesn't just inform you. It stands beside you as a witness when you need it: at a table where someone's being left out, at a moment you want to cheat, on a day you need courage. So the question today isn't which story is most important. It's which one stayed with you.
screen: `TEN GURUS, ONE LINE.` · `NANAK TO GOBIND SINGH.` · `THE GURU BECOMES THE GRANTH.` · `A SAKHI IS A WITNESS.` · then, large: `WHICH STORY STAYED?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: retell one story aloud. Settle, and breathe. Let the stories drift past, and wait for the one that tugs at you. Don't pick the one you think you should. Pick the one that stayed. Now tell it, out loud if you can, softly, in your own words, as if to a child. It's fine to forget details. Just tell what happened and why it matters to you. Then sit with it for a while in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. The year's stories: ten Gurus, the sakhis, the Khalsa's birth, and the one that stayed with you.
Your line: which story stayed. Today, tell that story to one person, at a meal, on a call, or in a message. Day three hundred twenty-six.

327.title: Looking back: the practices
327.hook: seva, kirtan, langar, simran, Nitnem and the gurdwara: which one you kept
327.howItsDone: Sikhs weave seva, kirtan, langar, simran and Nitnem into ordinary days and gather at the gurdwara; many describe Guru Nanak's three pillars, naam japna, kirat karni and vand chhakna, as the frame that holds them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the stories: ten Gurus, the sakhis, and your line, which story stayed. Did you tell it to someone? Today, we look back at what you did with your hands and breath. Day three hundred twenty-seven.

Think of any habit that lasted. Not the ones you announced on the first of January, but the quiet ones that just stuck. A walk after dinner. A song you always hum while washing up. A way you say goodnight. Nobody forced them; they just fit. Camp three gave you a whole toolbox of Sikh practices, one after another, for two months. Most people don't keep all of them. They keep one or two, and those become theirs. Today: looking back, at the practices.
screen: `THE HABITS THAT JUST STUCK.` → `A WHOLE TOOLBOX.` → `ONE OR TWO BECOME YOURS.`

segments.voice: Let's open the toolbox. Seva: service with no audience. Minding shoes at the gurdwara door, washing a dish slowly, setting aside a tenth, teaching someone kindly. And the warning that came with it: when seva feeds the ego, it stops being seva. Kirtan: first just listening, then humming, then singing Waheguru to a simple tune, then one line, the rahao, the pause line that holds a hymn's center. Langar: sitting level on the floor in rows, rolling rotis, receiving with cupped hands, and feeding one person at home with no agenda. Simran: remembering the Name on the breath. Wahe on the in-breath, Guru on the out-breath. The early hours before dawn. And the mind running off, again and again, and the practice being only to come back. Nitnem: the daily banis. Japji at dawn, Rehras at dusk, Kirtan Sohila at night, and the reminder that a starter Nitnem is an invitation, not a test. And the gurdwara: covering your head, taking off your shoes, bowing to the Word, the warm karah prashad in your hands, the hukamnama read from wherever the Granth falls open. Sikhs don't treat these as separate hobbies. They're one life: the Guru's word sung, remembered, served and shared. Sikhs often sum up Guru Nanak's teaching in three pillars that hold them up: remember the Name, earn honestly, share what you have. But a path is walked one step at a time, and most people find that one practice becomes a door to the others. So which one stuck for you? Not which one should have. Which one did?
screen: `SEVA WITHOUT AN AUDIENCE.` · `KIRTAN, LANGAR, SIMRAN.` · `NITNEM AND THE GURDWARA.` · `ONE PRACTICE OPENS THE OTHERS.` · then, large: `THE PRACTICE THAT STUCK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do the one you kept. Settle, and choose. If it was simran, breathe Wahe in, Guru out. If it was kirtan, hum a line you remember. If it was seva or langar, picture the task you'll do later today, and do it now in your mind, slowly and well. If it was Nitnem, say the first line you know. If nothing stuck yet, just breathe and let one of them choose you. Whatever it is, give it the whole two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. The year's practices: seva, kirtan, langar, simran, Nitnem and the gurdwara, and the one that became yours.
Your line: the practice that stuck. Today, do your kept practice once more, at the same time you'll do it tomorrow. Day three hundred twenty-seven.

328.title: Looking back: the Japji
328.hook: thirty-eight pauris heard and understood, one by one
328.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite the Japji every morning as the first of the daily banis, from memory or from a gutka, and it opens the Guru Granth Sahib itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the practices: seva, kirtan, langar, simran, Nitnem, and your line, the practice that stuck. Did you do it again? Today, the longest climb of the year: the Japji. Day three hundred twenty-eight.

Here's something most people never do in their lives: read a whole scripture slowly, line by line, sound first and meaning second. You did that. For seventy-five days, camp four walked through Guru Nanak's Japji, the first words of the Guru Granth Sahib and the first prayer of a Sikh morning. You said the openings aloud, in Gurmukhi, even when your tongue tripped. Then you learned what they meant. Somewhere in the middle, it may have stopped feeling like homework. Today: looking back, at the Japji.
screen: `A WHOLE SCRIPTURE, SLOWLY.` → `SOUND FIRST, MEANING SECOND.` → `SEVENTY-FIVE DAYS.`

segments.voice: It began before the first pauri, with the Mool Mantar: Ik Onkar, Satnam, one Creator, whose name is truth, without fear, without hate, beyond time, never born, self-existent, known by the Guru's grace. Then the salok: true in the beginning, true through the ages, true now, and true forever. Then pauri one, and its first line, which you said aloud: sochai soch na hovaee je sochee lakh vaar. Thinking a hundred thousand times won't get you there. The way through is hukam, walking in the order. Then pauri two: everything comes by that order, and whoever understands it stops saying I, I. After that, the great runs. Suniai: by listening. Mannai: by trusting. Asankh: countless, countless prayers and countless fools, and Nanak unworthy to count them. Then the realms, one after another, like a ladder: duty, knowledge, effort, grace, and at the top, the realm of truth, where the Formless dwells. And pauri thirty-eight, the mint: jat paahaaraa dheeraj suniaar. Let restraint be the furnace and patience the goldsmith, and there the Word is minted. And last, the salok that closes it: pavan guru paanee pitaa maataa dharat mahat. Air the Guru, water the father, earth the great mother. From thinking you can't get there, to seeing the whole world as your family. That's the arc of the Japji. And here is the plain truth worth saying out loud: you read it. Many people who grew up hearing it every morning never went through it line by line. That's not a boast. It's a gift you gave yourself, one pauri at a time.
screen: `THE MOOL MANTAR AND AAD SACH.` · `PAURI 1: THINKING CAN'T REACH.` · `LISTENING, TRUSTING, THE REALMS.` · `THE MINT, AND AIR, WATER, EARTH.` · then, large: `I READ IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read your favorite pauri. Settle, and think back through the Japji. Which pauri stayed with you? The first one, about overthinking? Listening? The countless? The mint? If you can, find it, and read it slowly, the Gurmukhi sound if you can manage it, then the meaning. If you can't look it up now, just say what you remember of it. Then sit with it, and let it be yours for a while. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. The Japji: Mool Mantar, thirty-eight pauris and the closing salok, heard and understood, one by one.
Your line: I read it. Today, tell one person, simply, that you read the Japji this year, and share the one line that stayed. Day three hundred twenty-eight.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Japji is a long morning prayer.
what it means: a journey from 'thinking can't reach it' to seeing air, water and earth as family, one pauri at a time.
what a scholar hears: the Japji has the Mool Mantar, an opening salok, 38 pauris and a closing salok, on angs 1–8; the closing salok is also attributed to Guru Angad.

329.title: Looking back: the depths
329.hook: themes, Bhagats, rehat, history and grief carried carefully
329.howItsDone: Sikhs deepen their understanding through katha (explanation of the hymns), study of the Guru Granth Sahib and Sikh history, and remembrance of the panth's struggles in the daily Ardas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the Japji: from sochai soch to air, water and earth, and your line, I read it. Today, the last and deepest stretch of the year: camp five, the depths. Day three hundred twenty-nine.

Think of swimming out past where your feet can touch the bottom. At first there's a small jolt of fear. The water gets darker and colder. Then, if you keep your breath steady, something changes. You're held up. You can see the shore behind you, and it looks small. Camp five was that kind of water. A hundred days past where the feet can touch: the Granth's biggest ideas, the Bhagats, the Sikh way of life, centuries of history, and a week of real grief. Today: looking back, at the depths.
screen: `PAST WHERE YOUR FEET TOUCH.` → `DARKER, COLDER, THEN HELD UP.` → `A HUNDRED DAYS OF DEEP WATER.`

segments.voice: It began with the shape of the Guru Granth Sahib: fourteen hundred thirty pages, each called an ang, a limb; many voices, one Guru. Then the great themes: hukam, the order; haumai, the ego that is its own disease and holds its own cure; naam, the Name; nadar, the kindly glance of grace. The five thieves in the house of the mind, and the five virtues that guard it. The Guru asking why woman should be called lesser, when kings are born of her. Asking about the light in a person, not their caste. Then the Bhagats: Kabir the weaver and Farid the Sufi, whose hymns the Gurus kept beside their own. Then rehat, the Sikh way of life: kesh, kangha, kara, kachhera and kirpan, amrit, the written code, and the many ways of being Sikh. The saint-soldier. Then the long history: Banda Singh, the years in the forests, the two ghallugharas, Ranjit Singh's golden temple, annexation, Jallianwala Bagh, the peaceful struggle for the gurdwaras, Partition, and a door opening at Kartarpur. Then 1984, carried as carefully as we could. And the diaspora, strangers who became neighbors everywhere. The Guru Granth Sahib often pictures the world as a vast, frightening ocean, the bhavjal, and the Guru's word as the boat that carries you across. That's a fair picture of camp five. Some of it was beautiful and wide open. Some of it was dark and cold and hard to look at. You didn't have to cross it alone, and you didn't have to understand everything. You just kept swimming, a day at a time. Deep water, crossed.
screen: `THE GRANTH'S SHAPE AND THEMES.` · `THE BHAGATS AND THE REHAT.` · `HISTORY, AND GRIEF CARRIED.` · `THE BOAT ACROSS THE OCEAN.` · then, large: `DEEP WATER, CROSSED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with what was hard. Settle, and let your breath steady. Let one hard part of this year's path come back to you. A teaching that challenged you. A story that hurt to hear. A question you still can't answer. Don't try to fix it or solve it. Just let it sit beside you, like a companion on a long swim. Notice that you're still here, still breathing, held up. Then let it rest. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. Camp five, the depths: the Granth's themes, the Bhagats, rehat, history, and grief carried carefully.
Your line: deep water, crossed. Today, when something feels too deep, remember you've already crossed deep water this year, one day at a time. Day three hundred twenty-nine.

the Guru's word, like a boat.

fork.reveal: the hymns picture the world as the bhavjal and the Guru's word as the boat that carries you over.

original.note: Gurmukhi: bhavjal, the world-ocean; in the hymns, the Guru's word is the boat across it.

trapdoor: what you thought: camp five was a list of hard topics.
what it means: deep water, the Granth's ideas, the way of life, history and grief, crossed a day at a time.
what a scholar hears: the ocean-and-boat image (bhavjal, bhausagar; the Guru as boat or ship) recurs across the Guru Granth Sahib, from Guru Nanak to the Bhagats.
